text:
My father’s suitcase contained three white dinner jackets and a bottle of morphine. The jackets were arranged in tissue paper. The morphine was inside a sock.

“Customs,” he explained.

“Is it illegal?”

“No. But I prefer not to begin a vacation with an account of my organs.”

He had always packed as though arriving somewhere were a form of vindication. My mother said this was because he had grown up poor. My father said it was because he had grown up in New Jersey.

I was fourteen. My suitcase contained seven black T-shirts and shorts I intended to wear over my bathing suit under all circumstances. We were going on a cruise: seven days, three islands, eleven hundred gay men. According to the booking agent, there would also be “a lovely family contingent.”

“How many is a contingent?” I asked.

“More than a delegation. Fewer than a problem.”

I had known my father was gay since I was nine. Before that, I had known things without knowing what they added up to. He slept in the guest room. My mother cried while putting away groceries. A man named Stephen could call during dinner.

After the divorce, my father and Stephen bought a sofa I wasn’t permitted to eat on. On alternate weekends I visited with my schoolbag.

At school, I called Stephen my father’s roommate. When my father found out, he asked whether I thought Stephen minded having to hide his toothbrush.

By fourteen, I said “my dad and his partner” in a voice intended to make further questions seem unsophisticated. Still, his world felt like a country where I possessed a passport but no fluency.

Then he became ill, and the language grew harder.

There were scans and treatments. Stephen, who taught architectural history, learned about blood counts. My father lost weight. Adults stopped speaking when I entered rooms, which made me want to enter every room in the world.

By February, the doctors had become interested in his comfort.

The cruise was his idea. Stephen couldn’t come; his mother had fallen in Tucson. My mother offered to join us.

“Darling,” my father said, “I’ve spent twenty years trying to avoid a family cruise.”

She laughed, then turned away.

***

Our cabin had a balcony and a bathroom in which you could touch every wall without moving your feet. Two towel swans occupied the bed.

“Already a more stable marriage than mine,” my father said.

At the safety drill, a crew member explained what to do if someone fell overboard.

“Point continuously.”

I had imagined rescue involving speed and equipment. Instead, one of your duties was not to lose sight of the person in the water.

At dinner, my father wore the first white jacket. Its sleeves had become too wide. We shared a table with six men.

“This is my daughter, Nora,” he said. “She is tolerating me.”

“That’s the nicest thing a fourteen-year-old can do,” said Len.

His husband, Arthur, adjusted every piece of silverware before eating. There were also two men named Michael and two who had met that afternoon and seemed uncertain whether they were now obliged to spend the week together.

Arthur asked what we were reading at school.

“*The Giver*.”

“Can a society eliminate pain without eliminating choice?”

“Our teacher mostly asks us to identify themes.”

“A mercy,” said one Michael.

My father ate some bread and a little soup. Nobody commented. Len asked about his jacket.

“Ancient,” my father said.

“Then there’s hope for all of us.”

For the first time since boarding, I stopped counting what he ate.

***

The next morning, while my father slept, I went to the pool.

There were bodies television seemed not to know about: enormous stomachs, scars, loose skin, a man whose prosthetic leg rested beneath a chair.

I kept my shorts on.

A boy was reading a paperback with a dragon on it. He wore an orange wristband like mine, meaning nobody could serve us alcohol.

I sat two chairs away.

“You can have that one,” he said. “Nobody’s using it.”

“I wasn’t worried.”

“O.K.”

His name was Eli. He was fifteen and lived near Philadelphia with two dads and a cat named Linda.

“Who are you with?” he asked.

“My dad.”

“Just your dad?”

“Yeah.”

He put a finger between his pages.

“The soft-serve machine on Deck Nine works twenty-four hours a day. I checked at six.”

We went to investigate.

Until then, conversations with boys had happened mostly at school, where any sentence could be used against you. I spoke in irritated efficiency, even to boys I had spent the evening imagining might speak to me.

Eli asked whether I preferred chocolate or vanilla.

“Both.”

“Good. That’s correct.”

One of his dads, Peter, had complained about the coffee. His other dad, Ben, had brought his own coffee and an apparatus for preparing it.

“Do they get along?” I asked.

“Mostly. Why?”

“I don’t know.”

He looked toward the water.

“Want to go to the arcade?”

I did.

***

By the third day, people knew my name. Len saved seats for us. Arthur found me a novel. A bartender kept ginger ale aside because it helped my father’s stomach.

I had expected to be invisible or permanently on display. Instead, I was remembered in small, useful ways.

Some people overdid it. One man asked whether I was “handling everything O.K.” with an expression that required me to comfort him.

“You needn’t issue progress reports,” my father said.

He was sitting on the bed, waiting for nausea to pass.

“Should I get someone?”

“No.”

“Dad.”

“Nora, I’m having a bad half hour. Let me have it.”

I went onto the balcony, furious. Below us, white water followed the ship. It seemed impossible that something so large could keep moving without apparent effort.

Eventually he joined me.

“I’m sorry.”

“It’s fine.”

“It isn’t, but thank you.”

We watched the water.

“How’s Eli?”

“He’s just a person.”

“A rare quality.”

“Please don’t.”

“All right.”

He closed his eyes.

“You don’t have to stay in the cabin because I do.”

I didn’t answer. It seemed wrong that he could send me away and make me feel guilty for staying.

***

At the first island, I went ashore with Eli and his dads. My father watched from our balcony. I could distinguish his white shirt, but not his face.

I raised my arm. He raised his.

We visited a fort, then a beach. Peter read aloud from a guidebook until Ben suggested the fort might like some privacy.

At the water, Eli asked, “Is your dad sick?”

I stared at him.

“Sorry. You don’t have to—”

“He has cancer. It’s not the kind you get better from.”

He nodded. He didn’t tell me about a relative or ask whether I had tried being positive.

“Want to go back?”

“Not yet.”

We waded in. My shorts ballooned, then clung to my legs. A fish flicked past Eli’s knee, and he made a noise so undignified I laughed.

“Shark,” he said.

“It was the size of a leaf.”

“A young shark.”

For an hour, I forgot to wonder what my father was doing.

Back in the cabin, he slept beside a half-eaten sandwich. His watch lay next to the morphine.

When he woke, I told him about the fish. He laughed, and I felt I had brought him something.

***

On the fifth day, there was a tea dance.

I had thought tea would be involved. Instead, several hundred men danced in the afternoon heat. My father sat beneath an awning with Len and Arthur.

Eli and I stood eating fries.

“Do you dance?” he asked.

“No.”

“Me neither.”

One Michael approached.

“You look like restaurant inspectors.”

“We’re observing,” I said.

“Observe closer.”

He led us onto the dance floor, then abandoned us.

My elbows seemed newly attached. Eli bent his knees experimentally. We laughed, and after that it became possible.

Nobody watched for long. Men danced alone, couples held each other, friends shouted lyrics. Across the deck, my father tapped a finger against his knee.

I had watched him become more himself at parties: quicker, louder, making strangers laugh at stories I’d already heard. I had resented his audiences.

Now he caught my eye and made an elaborate approving gesture, as though I were accomplishing more than moving from foot to foot.

I rolled my eyes. He smiled.

That evening, Eli kissed me outside the closed jewelry shop.

We had been arguing about whether anyone bought paintings at the ship’s art auctions. He said his grandfather had bought a horse.

“A painting of a horse?”

“Unfortunately.”

Then he asked, “Can I kiss you?”

I hadn’t known a boy could ask. I thought it was something you had to recognize just before it happened, like a ball approaching your face.

“Yes.”

The kiss mostly involved the corner of my mouth.

“Was that O.K.?”

“Yes.”

We examined a diamond necklace revolving in the window.

I wanted to tell someone. I wanted to tell no one, ever.

Back in the cabin, my father was watching a nature program.

“Nice evening?”

“Fine.”

I could see him deciding not to ask. I loved him for it.

***

The next day, my father stayed in bed until late afternoon. Standing, he had to wait before taking a step. I had learned to look away while remaining close enough to help.

“We could skip dinner,” I said.

“And deprive them of the third jacket?”

“Nobody’s counting.”

“I am.”

His hands trembled, so I fastened his cuff links, silver squares Stephen had given him.

At dinner, Len described playing a tree in a school production.

“A speaking tree,” Arthur said.

“Only because I refused to be silenced.”

My father laughed, then coughed into his napkin. Conversation continued. The waiter replenished the bread.

When my father went to the bathroom, Len leaned toward me.

“Does he have everything he needs?”

“I think so.”

“And do you?”

I studied my plate.

Len waited.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s a perfectly good answer.”

He moved the bread basket closer.

***

The last night was formal. There were photographers at every staircase and a sunset of embarrassing competence.

My father wore the first jacket again. The second was stained; the third, he said, had never suited him.

After dinner, we joined our friends in a lounge. Beyond the windows, there was nothing except our reflections.

Eli asked if I wanted to walk around.

“In a minute.”

“Sure.”

He touched my shoulder.

“He seems kind,” my father said.

“He is.”

“That’s useful.”

The band began a song my father used to play while cooking, turning from the stove to sing the important parts to Stephen.

“Dance with me.”

“Are you sure?”

“It’s a slow song.”

“I’m bad.”

“So am I. We’ll cancel each other out.”

He braced a hand against the table and stood.

Under the jacket, he felt smaller than he looked. He held my hand loosely, leaving me to decide how firmly to hold his.

We moved a little.

“No expertise required,” he said.

There was a shaving cut beneath his jaw. I wanted to ask who would teach me to drive. I wanted to ask whether he was afraid. I wanted him to say something sufficiently large that I could live on it afterward.

Instead, I said, “You’re stepping on me.”

“Then you know it’s authentic.”

His hand tightened against my back.

“Tired?” I asked.

“A little.”

“We can stop.”

“In a minute.”

I could feel each breath beneath my hand. He was making an effort. I was too. Nobody watching could have said which of us was holding up the other.

When the song ended, he didn’t immediately let go.

“Thank you.”

“You asked me.”

“Yes,” he said. “I did.”

***

He died five weeks after we got home.

Stephen had returned from Tucson. My mother drove me across town every afternoon and waited downstairs.

Eli and I wrote daily, then less often. He sent photographs of Linda. We didn’t become people who crossed great distances for each other, but for a time his name on my phone could alter an afternoon.

In June, Stephen gave me the cuff links. I wanted them, although I had no cuffs.

For years, I remembered the last dance so often that certain details became uncertain. Once, in a store, I thought I heard the song. I stopped beside some towels. Then the chorus came, and it wasn’t.

Other things stayed clear.

On our last morning aboard, my father slept in a chair with our documents in his lap. Around us, men exchanged addresses and embraced people they had met seven days earlier.

Eli hugged me, then shook my father’s hand.

“Have his number?” my father asked afterward.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He closed his eyes. I held our passports. When a crew member asked whether we needed assistance, I said we were all right for the moment.
